lens: H — the D-010 verifier (`verifier/**` + the `fixtures/samples` bundles it certifies), hunting LIVE certification defects rather than surviving mutations.

findings.title: A-055's trust-root repair closed the DEMONSTRATION, not the ARGUMENT: the presenter still chooses the trust root, one directory up — and the check added to stop it affirmatively states the opposite
findings.surface: verifier/verify.py:_find_domain (lines 76-131) and the Check constructed at lines 195-205
findings.claim: `_find_domain` distinguishes two PATHS (bundle dir vs parent dir), not two PROVENANCES. A presenter who ships a directory tree — `tree/domain.json` + `tree/bundle/` — supplies the parent copy, so `_find_domain` returns it labelled `deployment copy (parent directory)`, `domain_presenter_supplied` is False, and the verifier prints `[PASS] the trust root is the deployment's, not the presenter's`. A-055's own docstring states the invariant as 'THE PRESENTER OF A BUNDLE MUST NOT CHOOSE THE TRUST ROOT'; that invariant is still violated. The exploit is byte-for-byte A-055's O-2, moved up one directory: a receipt re-signed with an arbitrary outsider key, `receipt.signer` rewritten to that key's address, a `domain.json` naming it — `=> PASS`, exit 0. `--all` on the presenter's tree prints `1/1 sample(s) verified`, exit 0. This is failure mode 3 from the standing brief (a repair that generalises the demonstration) applied to the very finding that round was written to close.
findings.why_it_matters: `domain.signerAddress` is the only thing binding a receipt to the deployment's signer rather than to whoever signed it; every downstream signer check is relative to it. The verifier's headline claim is independent third-party certification, and the one shape in which a receipt actually reaches a third party — a directory handed over by the party who wants it believed — is the shape the fix does not cover. Worse than a silent gap: the verifier now emits an affirmative PASS line asserting the provenance it did not establish, so a reader who checks for exactly this is told it was checked.

findings.title: The §5.5 override stage has NO deployment-anchored owner identity check: an override minted by an arbitrary outsider key, payload byte-identical to the owner's, verifies => PASS with the real domain.json
findings.claim: `_override_checks` verifies that the override signature recovers the SELF-DECLARED `override.json:ownerAddress`, and that the recovered address is not the Sentinel signer (§3.3(7)). Nothing binds the authorizing party to any identity the presenter did not supply. `domain.json` carries no owner field and is never consulted for one; `mandate.principal` — which REPORT.md line 174 states IS the ownerAddress, and which D-030/§5.1 tie to the vault owner — is never read by verify.py at all (`grep -n principal verifier/verify.py` returns nothing). The receipt path has `recovered signer == domain.json signerAddress`; the §5.5.1 refusal path has `the recovered signer is the deployment's Sentinel signer`, carrying a comment that says in as many words 'a self-declared signer is not an identity. Anyone can mint a record naming their own key and sign it, and every check above passes.' That sentence is true of the override stage today and there is no check there that answers it. §3.3(7)'s `recovered != receipt.signer` passes trivially for any third party and is the ONLY party check in the stage. A-055 fixed this class on two of the three signed artifacts; the third was not reached.
findings.why_it_matters: The override is the credential that makes a REVIEW receipt executable — §5.5, and §3.3(7) calls it the credential the isolated signer must not be able to mint. The verifier prints `=> PASS`, exit 0, over a bundle whose owner authorization was minted by someone who is neither the owner nor the signer, with every override check green including the one named for §3.3(7). The on-chain vault presumably still enforces its own owner, so this is a defect in what D-010 CERTIFIES, not necessarily an on-chain bypass — but D-010 exists precisely so a third party need not trust the chain operator's word, and here it certifies a forged credential as authorized. It is the same class as the two live defects the previous round scored as its best findings.

findings.title: A-055's signerFindings repair used PRECEDENCE, not both: one added key inside the envelope re-opens the exact hole it closed, and an uncommitted reason code passes with [PASS] signerFindings ⊆ the committed reason-code set
findings.surface: verifier/verify.py:_refusal_reason_code_checks (lines 977-1000, the `findings = source.get(...)` / `if findings is None: findings = receipt_doc.get(...)` pair)
findings.claim: A-055's O-1 finding was that `signerFindings` resolved to None on the repository's one refusal artifact, so the subset invariant silently skipped. The repair resolves findings from the refusal envelope FIRST and falls back to `receipt_doc` only when the envelope key is ABSENT. Absent is not the same as trustworthy: adding `"signerFindings": []` inside `refusalRecord` shadows the top-level array — the array the shipped corpus actually uses, and the array the repair was written for — so `missing` is computed over an empty set and the check passes vacuously. The identical precedence applies to `reasonCodes`, so the top-level `reasonCodes` a reader sees can be a completely different list from the one hashed, and the verifier still prints `1 code(s) committed` and `=> PASS`. The repair generalised A-055's demonstration (the key being missing) rather than its argument (a presenter must not choose which of two co-located arrays is invariant-checked).
findings.why_it_matters: §5.4/D-022's committed set is the union of the evaluator's codes and the signer's findings; the subset check is the only thing preventing a refusal from carrying signer findings the signature does not commit to. The bundle in the reproduction advertises `SIGNER_OWNER_APPROVED_OUT_OF_BAND` in the array a dashboard or operator reads, that code is not in the committed set, and the verifier certifies the bundle and prints the subset check as satisfied. The printed line carries no detail naming WHICH array it checked — unlike the skip branch, which was given the explicit 'checked both (A-055)' wording.

findings.probe_moved_something: The delta between the probe and its control is exactly one JSON key, and it moves the named check from [FAIL] to [PASS] and the process from exit 1 to exit 0. That is the strongest possible liveness evidence for this probe: the check demonstrably fires on the same bundle without the shadow key.

findings.title: On the receipt path a payload-hash FAILURE becomes a PASS when the contradicting file is DELETED — `rm action.json` flips exit 1 to exit 0; the refusal path treats the same absence as a failure and says why
findings.surface: verifier/verify.py:_payload_hash_check (line 1146, `if doc is None: return Check(..., True, 'payload file not present in this sample', skipped=True)`) and _binding_checks (line 1078) vs _refusal_binding_checks (lines 878-889)
findings.claim: When `mandate.json` / `policy.json` / `action.json` are absent, every payload-hash recomputation and the whole §3.3(4)/§5.8 chain-and-vault binding stage become skipped-as-passed and the bundle certifies `=> PASS`, exit 0. So a presenter holding a genuine signed receipt for action A, caught out when action.json for action B fails the actionHash check, converts the failure into a pass by deleting the file. The refusal path already rejects exactly this reasoning: 'the bundle carries no action.json, so the action this refusal names cannot be exhibited... a record whose actionHash matches nothing in front of the verifier is attributable to the signer but not to this bundle... Treated as a failure rather than a skip: see REPORT.md F-18.5.' Every word of that applies verbatim to a receipt, and the receipt path does the opposite.
findings.why_it_matters: This is 'not checked sums as passed' with an attacker-controlled trigger — the presenter chooses whether the check runs, by choosing what to include. The receipt's own EIP-712 domain still binds chain and vault, so the bundle is not unbound; but a receipt whose mandateHash/policyHash/actionHash are exhibited against nothing is certified `=> PASS` and the exit status a CI harness reads is 0. The SKIP lines are printed, so a human reading the full output is not lied to — the defect is that the aggregate verdict and exit code do not reflect them, and that the two paths in the same file resolve the identical question in opposite directions.

cd <worktree>
  P=/private/.../scratchpad/probe-h
  mkdir -p $P/p3 && cp fixtures/samples/domain.json $P/p3/ && cp -R fixtures/samples/case-1-allow $P/p3/b
  cp fixtures/samples/case-3-wrong-purpose-block/action.json $P/p3/b/action.json
  python3 -B verifier/verify.py $P/p3/b >/dev/null 2>&1 ; echo EXIT=$?
    -> EXIT=1   ([FAIL] recomputed actionHash from §5.3 ActionPayload matches the receipt
                 computed 0x5914da90...  declared 0x6f630833...)
  rm $P/p3/b/action.json
  python3 -B verifier/verify.py $P/p3/b >/dev/null 2>&1 ; echo EXIT=$?
    -> EXIT=0   ([SKIP] recomputed actionHash from §5.3 ActionPayload / payload file not present
                 in this sample ... => PASS)
Stripping all three payload files from an otherwise untouched case-1-allow gives:
  [SKIP] §3.3(4) chain and vault binding — no §5.1-§5.3 payload file in this sample
  [SKIP] recomputed mandateHash / policyHash / actionHash ...   => PASS, 1/1 verified, EXIT=0
findings.probe_moved_something: The same bundle, differing by the presence of one file, produces exit 1 with a [FAIL] line naming two concrete hashes and then exit 0 with a [SKIP] line in its place. Both states were observed; the check is live in the first.

findings.title: `_verdict_check` and `_refusal_label_check` print 'no meta.json/index.json to cross-check against' about a bundle that carries meta.json
findings.claim: Both functions read `meta.json`, then fall back to the parent's `index.json`, then emit a SKIP whose detail asserts 'no meta.json/index.json to cross-check against'. The condition actually tested is `expected is None`, which is also satisfied when meta.json is present and merely lacks the `verdict` / `signerRefused` key. The verifier then states something false about the artifact in front of it — the same defect shape as A-055's O-1 ('printed "the bundle carries no signerFindings array" about a bundle that carries one').
findings.why_it_matters: Low consequence: the receipt verdict is separately bound to the evidence bundle via `evidence.verdict agrees with the receipt's verdict enum`, so nothing certifies wrongly. It matters as an instrument-honesty defect in a project whose stated failure mode is exactly this, and because the corrective wording pattern already exists three functions away ('checked both (A-055)').

findings.title: `test_owner_is_the_mandate_principal` is a fourth instance of the corpus-property/verifier-property category error A-056 named as 'THE CATEGORY ERROR IS THE FINDING' — and it is the ONLY assertion anywhere of the relation H-2 shows the verifier never evaluates
findings.claim: A-056 named three tests with this shape (`test_only_review_receipts_carry_an_override`, `test_owner_is_not_the_sentinel_signer`, `test_review_receipt_hash_is_the_receipt_hashstruct`) and fixed the first with a constructed-artifact test. `test_owner_is_the_mandate_principal` sits between the other two, was not named, and is the purest instance of the four: it opens the fixture's override.json and mandate.json and asserts `ownerAddress.lower() == principal.lower()`. It states a property of the repository. `verify.py` never reads `mandate.principal` at all. A reader auditing coverage sees a test whose NAME asserts the owner-identity relation and will reasonably conclude the verifier enforces it; it does not, which is H-2.
findings.why_it_matters: The category error A-056 declared as the round's finding is still live in the same class, in the same test class, three lines from one of the instances it named — and the surviving instance is the one whose absent verifier-side counterpart is the CRITICAL of this round. It is direct evidence that fixing the named instances did not fix the pattern, which is the argument-vs-demonstration failure applied to the instrument layer.
findings.reproduction:
grep -n 'def test_owner_is_the_mandate_principal' -A4 verifier/test_verifier.py
    950:    def test_owner_is_the_mandate_principal(self):
    951:        doc = self._doc()
    952:        mandate = read_json(OVERRIDE_SAMPLE, "mandate.json")
    953:        self.assertEqual(doc["ownerAddress"].lower(), mandate["principal"].lower())
  grep -n 'principal' verifier/verify.py   ->  (no output)
  grep -n 'principal' verifier/eip712.py   ->  58:    ("address", "principal")   [struct field only]
The test passes against the H-2 exploit bundle unchanged, because the exploit does not touch the shipped fixture — which is the whole point: a fixture property cannot see a verifier that accepts what the fixture does not contain.
findings.probe_moved_something: The grep for `principal` over verify.py returning empty is the moved artifact: it is a positive, checkable absence, and it is what makes the test's name a claim the code does not honour. Cross-checked against H-2's live run, where the owner is a key with no relation to mandate.principal and every override check is [PASS].

brief_critique:
The lens brief was well aimed and its central instruction was correct: it told me to stop hunting surviving mutations and hunt live certification defects, it named the two shapes the last round found, and it said "find the third." There were three, and all three are in the shapes it named — presenter-chosen trust root, a self-declared identity nothing anchors, and an invariant that resolves to the wrong array. Two specific credits: the warning that a probe can be dead saved me from at least one wrong conclusion (I ran controls on every finding and Control C on H-1 is what proves H-1 is not an artifact of my key generation), and the instruction to look at "every place it prints a conclusion about what it examined" is what turned H-1 from "a residual gap" into "the verifier states the opposite of the truth", which is the version worth reporting.

Three criticisms.

(1) THE SCOPE LINE IS PHRASED IN A WAY THAT INVITES THE PROJECT'S OWN NAMED CATEGORY ERROR. It reads: "`verifier/**` ... together with the samples under `fixtures/` that it certifies." Every finding above required a CONSTRUCTED artifact that is not in `fixtures/` and that the corpus deliberately does not contain — an outsider-signed override, a shadowed `signerFindings`, a bundle with `action.json` removed. A reviewer who read "the samples under fixtures/ that it certifies" as the probe surface would have swept the shipped corpus, found everything green, and returned a null. That is `test_only_review_receipts_carry_an_override` at the level of the review brief: a fixture property cannot catch a verifier that accepts what the fixture does not contain, and A-056 already named this as "THE CATEGORY ERROR IS THE FINDING". The brief should say that the probe surface is the space of artifacts the verifier will ACCEPT, and that `fixtures/` is a starting point to mutate away from, not the boundary.

(2) THE BRIEF POINTED AT verify.py AND fixtures/, AND THE ROUND'S CRITICAL NEEDED docs/decisions.md AND verifier/REPORT.md TO BE SCORED HONESTLY. H-2 is only a defect rather than an unavoidable limitation because `mandate.principal` exists in the bundle, is hash-committed, and is identified as the ownerAddress in REPORT.md line 174 and tied to the vault owner in D-030. Without reading outside the assigned target I would have had to report H-2 as "the verifier structurally cannot know the owner", which is the wrong finding. The brief's list of what to read (v1-1-register, decisions A-045..A-056) was framed as a map of already-covered ground to avoid, not as evidence — and here it was evidence.

(3) A SMALLER ONE, AND IT IS TO THE BRIEF'S CREDIT. The brief says verify.py is 1830 lines. Four places in the repository — including `scripts/test.sh:557`, which the gate prints — say 1681. The brief is right and the artifact is stale (H-7). Worth noting because the brief's instrument-check instruction assumes the brief is the likely error; this time it was the only correct copy.

One thing I did NOT find wrong: the brief's environment facts were all accurate as far as I exercised them (no `.env`, `ts/node_modules` a symlink, `python3 -B` needed). I never needed Foundry or the corpus runner.

SWEPT TO THE BOTTOM. `verify.py` was read line by line, all 1830 lines, and I traced every path by which a `Check` can be constructed with `ok=True` or `skipped=True` — that enumeration is where H-1, H-4, H-5 and H-8 came from. I specifically walked: the trust-root resolution (`_find_domain`), both artifact paths (§5.4 receipt and §5.5.1 refusal) including which checks each path runs and which it never reaches, `_locate_refusal`/`_extract_refusal`'s shape acceptance including the depth-2 descent and the flat-vs-nested leftover asymmetry, both reason-code stages, `_binding_checks`, `_payload_hash_check`, `_chain_checks`, `_override_checks`, `_verdict_check`/`_refusal_label_check`, and `main`/`run`/`run_tamper_suite`. `refusal.py` and `reasoncodes.py` were read in full and their validation is genuinely strict in both directions (missing AND extra fields rejected; `fullmatch` with the anchors deliberately removed) — I probed for a way past `canonical_fields` and did not find one.

MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Baseline on the untouched tree before any probe: 160/160 tests OK, 7/7 samples verified, exit 0. Tamper applicability matrix over all 29 modes x 7 samples: 77 applied, 126 N/A, no mode inapplicable on every sample — the published "77 cases over 29 modes" is accurate and there is no dead mode. `wc -l verify.py` = 1830 against four published 1681s.

PROBED AND CAME BACK CLEAN — reporting these as nulls because a null from a probe is different from a null from silence. `jcs.parse_bytes` rejects duplicate object members and a UTF-8 BOM, so no key-shadowing attack through any JSON file the verifier reads. `receipt.json` shapes I tried and that all fail closed: `refused: true` beside a signed receipt; `receipt: null`; an empty-string signature; a refusal record beside a receipt body. The `--tamper override-signer-mints` and `--tamper refusal-wrongkey` paths behave as documented. `_refusal_checks`'s decision-OR-refusal mutual exclusion fires. `evidence.hash` and `evidence.canonical.json` are both bound to RECOMPUTED bytes, not to each other.

NOT TOUCHED, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT BOUNDS THE RESULT. (1) `fixtures/corpus/**` — 50 fixtures, eight labeller files, `_digests.json`, the frozen labelling prompt and its sha256 — was not examined AT ALL, and the lens's target line ("the samples under `fixtures/`") can be read to include it. If corpus integrity is in scope, that half is unswept. (2) `fixtures/injection/**` and `fixtures/d019-revisit/**` were deliberately not opened. (3) `eip712.py` (309 lines), `secp256k1.py` (172), `keccak.py` (106) were not read — I have no independent view of them, and register §9 records 24 of 41 latent survivors living in the first two. Any defect reachable only through their value-level validation is invisible to this report. (4) `test_verifier.py` is 2373 lines and I read about 150 of them; H-6 was found by grepping for one concept, and I did not systematically audit the other ~155 tests for the same corpus-property shape — given that I found a fourth instance by looking once, I would expect more and I did not look. (5) No mutation of verify.py, by design. (6) No full `./scripts/test.sh` run, no Foundry, no TypeScript suite, no corpus runner.

CONFIDENCE SHAPE. H-1, H-2, H-3 and H-4 are each demonstrated by a run on the unmutated tree WITH a control that flips the same named check the other way, so I am not relying on the absence of output anywhere. H-5, H-7 and H-8 are direct observations with no inference. H-6 is a code reading plus two greps. The weakest link in the whole report is H-2's dependence on `mandate.principal` being the owner, which I took from documentation and did not verify against the contracts — and H-2 survives as a finding even if that turns out false, because the stage has no owner anchor of ANY kind.
